q: What are the two fundamental data types in Azure Monitor?
exp: Azure Monitor stores two basic kinds of data: metrics (numeric values sampled over time, good for charts and fast alerts) and logs (records with many fields, stored in Log Analytics and queried with KQL). Alerts, dashboards, tags and locks are features built on top of them, not data types.

q: Where in the portal do you chart a VM's Percentage CPU over the last 24 hours?
exp: Azure Monitor → Metrics (Metrics explorer), or the Metrics blade on the VM itself, lets you chart platform metrics such as Percentage CPU for any time range, including the last 24 hours. The Activity log shows operations, Advisor gives recommendations and Cost analysis shows spend.

q: In Metrics explorer, how do you see storage transactions broken down by API name?
opts: Apply splitting on the ApiName dimension
Apply a filter on the Time range control
exp: Many metrics have dimensions. Applying splitting on the ApiName dimension of the Transactions metric draws a separate line for each API (GetBlob, PutBlob and so on). Changing the time range or pinning the chart doesn't break it down, and the Activity log doesn't hold metrics.

q: Which aggregation shows the highest CPU value in each time grain?
exp: The Max aggregation shows the highest value recorded in each time interval, so short CPU spikes stay visible. Avg smooths them out, Sum adds values together and Count counts samples, so neither is the peak.

q: How often are most platform metrics collected?
exp: Most Azure platform metrics are collected every minute (1-minute granularity), which makes them near real-time. Some metrics are collected less often, but 1 minute is the usual interval. It isn't hourly or daily, and 10-second collection isn't standard.

q: Which feature shares a set of charts with a team in the portal?
opts: Pin charts to an Azure dashboard (or use Workbooks) and share it
Export the charts to the Activity log and share its saved filter
exp: Pin charts to an Azure dashboard and share it — dashboards are Azure resources, so access is controlled with RBAC — or build a Workbook. Exporting the Activity log, budgets and locks don't share charts.

q: Which Azure Monitor feature combines text, KQL queries, metrics, and parameters into interactive reports?
exp: Azure Monitor Workbooks combine text, KQL queries, metrics and parameters into interactive reports that people can filter and drill into. Action groups send notifications, alert processing rules change alert actions, and DCRs define data collection.

q: Can you collect guest OS data such as free disk space or Windows events without an agent?
opts: No — guest OS data needs the Azure Monitor Agent
Yes — platform metrics include all guest OS data
exp: Platform metrics cover what Azure collects for the VM by itself, such as CPU, network, disk operations and available memory. Guest OS data such as free space on a disk or Windows events needs the Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule. That's the same for Windows and Linux, whatever the disk type.

q: What's a Log Analytics workspace?
opts: A unique environment for log data in Azure Monitor, with its own data, retention, and access configuration
A shared dashboard that stores chart definitions, alert rules, and metric data for one resource group
exp: A Log Analytics workspace is where Azure Monitor stores log data. Each workspace has its own data, retention settings, pricing tier and access control, and you query it with KQL. It isn't a VM, a storage container or a dashboard.

q: Which CLI command creates a Log Analytics workspace?
opts: az monitor log-analytics workspace create -g RG1 -n law1
az monitor workspace add -g RG1 -n law1 --type log-analytics
exp: az monitor log-analytics workspace create creates a Log Analytics workspace (with -g and -n, plus optional location, SKU and retention). The other commands don't exist.

q: Users should only see log data for resources they have access to, without workspace-wide permissions. Which access mode?
exp: With the workspace access control mode set to 'Use resource or workspace permissions', users can query logs in resource context: they see only data from resources they have Azure RBAC access to, without needing permissions on the whole workspace. Workspaces are never public, and shared keys are for agents, not users.

q: Which role lets a user read all workspace data and run queries but not change settings?
exp: Log Analytics Reader can view and query all data in a workspace and see its settings, but can't change anything. Log Analytics Contributor and Monitoring Contributor can change settings, and Owner can do everything.

q: Data must be kept 7 years for compliance but is rarely queried. Cheapest approach in Log Analytics?
opts: Long-term retention (archive) for older data, plus restore or search jobs when needed
Interactive retention for 7 years on every table, with a daily ingestion cap
exp: Log Analytics can keep data for up to 12 years with long-term retention, much more cheaply than interactive retention. You can't query it directly, but when needed you bring it back with a search job or a restore. Keeping 7 years interactive costs far more, and deleting after 30 days breaks compliance.

q: Ingestion is about 300 GB/day and stable. How do you reduce cost per GB?
opts: Use a commitment tier pricing level
Split the data over more workspaces
exp: Commitment tiers give a lower price per GB when you commit to a daily ingestion volume (for example 300 GB/day), which suits predictable workloads. Pay-as-you-go costs more at that volume. Creating more workspaces or increasing retention doesn't cut the cost per GB.

q: You want to cap ingestion to avoid surprise bills. Which workspace setting?
exp: A daily cap stops data collection in the workspace for the rest of the day once the limit is reached, which protects against surprise bills. The trade-off is that you lose data after the cap. Retention, access mode and data export don't limit ingestion.

q: Which CLI command creates a diagnostic setting sending a Key Vault's AuditEvent logs to a workspace?
exp: az monitor diagnostic-settings create sends a resource's logs to a destination: --resource is the key vault's ID, --workspace the Log Analytics workspace, and --logs lists the categories, here AuditEvent. Key vaults have no logging command of their own, and the other commands don't exist.

q: Diagnostic settings must be applied automatically to every new Key Vault in a subscription. Best approach?
opts: Azure Policy with a DeployIfNotExists diagnostic settings definition
An Activity log alert rule that runs when a Key Vault is created
exp: A built-in Azure Policy definition with the DeployIfNotExists effect can create the diagnostic setting automatically on every key vault, including new ones, and a remediation task fixes existing vaults. Configuring each vault by hand doesn't scale, and locks and alerts don't create settings.

q: Logs must stream to a third-party SIEM in near real time. Which destination?
exp: An Event Hub destination streams logs in near real time to external systems such as a third-party SIEM. A storage account is for cheaper long-term archive, and email and dashboards aren't diagnostic setting destinations.

q: How many diagnostic settings can a single resource have?
exp: Each resource can have up to 5 diagnostic settings — for example one to Log Analytics, one to storage and one to an Event Hub, each with different categories. It isn't limited to 1, and it isn't unlimited.

q: Who deleted VM1 yesterday? Where do you look first?
opts: Activity log, filtered on the delete operation
Metrics, filtered on the VM availability
exp: Deleting a VM is a control-plane operation, so the Activity log records it with the caller's identity, the time and the status. Filter it on the delete operation. VM insights, metrics and boot diagnostics show performance and console output, not who did what.

q: Which Activity log event categories exist?
opts: Administrative, Service Health, Resource Health, Alert, Autoscale, Recommendation, Security, Policy
Metrics, Logs, Traces, Changes, Heartbeat, Performance, Syslog, Custom tables and Events
exp: The Activity log has several categories: Administrative (create, update, delete), Service Health, Resource Health, Alert, Autoscale, Recommendation (from Advisor), Security (from Defender for Cloud) and Policy. It covers more than administrative operations, and it doesn't hold metrics.

q: Do blob uploads (data-plane operations) appear in the Activity log?
opts: No — only control-plane operations; data-plane operations need resource logs
Yes — control-plane and data-plane operations are both recorded for 90 days
exp: The Activity log records only control-plane operations, such as creating a storage account or changing its settings. Data-plane operations such as uploading, reading or deleting blobs need storage resource logs (StorageRead, StorageWrite, StorageDelete) sent through a diagnostic setting.

q: Which KQL operator chooses the columns in the output?
exp: project chooses which columns appear in the output, and can rename them (project Name = Computer). where filters rows, summarize aggregates them (count, avg and so on), and extend adds calculated columns while keeping the existing ones.

q: Which KQL query returns the 10 computers with the highest average CPU?
opts: Perf | where CounterName == "% Processor Time" | summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer | top 10 by avg_CounterValue desc
Perf | where CounterName == "% Processor Time" | order by CounterValue asc | summarize by Computer | limit 10 by avg desc
exp: First filter Perf to the CPU counter, then summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer to get each computer's average, then top 10 by avg_CounterValue desc to keep the ten highest. take 10 returns any ten rows, and SELECT TOP is SQL.

q: Which KQL operator adds a new calculated column?
exp: extend adds a new column calculated from an expression, for example extend CpuPercent = CounterValue / 100. project-away removes columns, join combines tables and render draws charts.

q: Which query shows Windows error events from the last 24 hours?
opts: Event | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and EventLevelName == "Error"
Syslog | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and SeverityLevel == "Windows"
exp: Windows event logs collected by the agent go to the Event table, so filter it with where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) and EventLevelName == "Error". Syslog is the Linux equivalent, and AzureActivity holds Azure control-plane operations.

q: Which KQL operator draws a timechart from query results?
exp: render timechart draws the query result as a line chart over time, usually after summarize ... by bin(TimeGenerated, ...). render also supports barchart, piechart, columnchart and others. plot, chart() and graph aren't KQL operators.

q: Which table holds Azure control-plane operations sent to a workspace from the Activity log?
exp: When the Activity log is sent to a Log Analytics workspace, its records go to the AzureActivity table, which holds caller, operation and status. AzureDiagnostics holds resource logs, Heartbeat holds agent heartbeats and Perf holds performance counters.

q: Which query finds VMs that haven't sent a heartbeat in the last 15 minutes?
opts: Heartbeat | summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer | where LastSeen < ago(15m)
Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated < ago(15m) | summarize LastSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by Computer
exp: summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer finds each computer's most recent heartbeat, and where LastSeen < ago(15m) keeps only computers whose last heartbeat is older than 15 minutes, meaning they've stopped reporting. The other queries return old rows or arbitrary rows rather than silent machines.

q: Order the KQL pipeline steps to chart average CPU per hour for one computer:
items: where Computer == "VM1" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
exp: Every KQL query starts with a table (Perf), then filters with where (the computer and counter), then aggregates with summarize ... by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) for hourly averages, and finally render timechart draws it. Each step works on the output of the step before.

q: What does a Data Collection Rule (DCR) define?
opts: What data to collect (events, counters, logs), from which machines, and where to send it
The alert thresholds, the action groups, and the time windows for each machine
exp: A data collection rule (DCR) tells the Azure Monitor Agent what to collect (Windows events, performance counters, Syslog, text logs), which machines it applies to (through DCR associations), any transformations, and where to send the data (for example a Log Analytics workspace). It doesn't define alerts, roles or backups.

q: How do you collect only Windows Security events with IDs 4624 and 4625 (to reduce cost) with AMA?
opts: Use an XPath query filter in the DCR's Windows event log data source
Collect all events and delete later
Set a daily cap on the workspace for the SecurityEvent table
exp: A DCR's Windows event log data source accepts XPath queries, such as Security!*[System[(EventID=4624 or EventID=4625)]], so the agent only collects those events and you pay for less data. Collecting everything and deleting later still costs ingestion, MMA is retired, and a daily cap drops data instead of filtering it.

q: Can one DCR be associated with many VMs, and can one VM have multiple DCRs?
exp: DCR associations are many-to-many: one DCR can be associated with many machines, and one machine can have several DCRs (for example a standard security DCR plus an app-specific one).

q: On-premises servers must send logs to Azure Monitor with AMA. What's required first?
opts: Onboard them to Azure Arc, then install AMA as an extension
Install the MMA agent, then upgrade it to AMA with a policy
exp: The Azure Monitor Agent runs on non-Azure machines only after they're onboarded to Azure Arc, which gives them an Azure identity and lets you install AMA as an extension. The legacy MMA agent is retired, and Network Watcher doesn't collect logs.

q: Which identity does the Azure Monitor Agent use to authenticate when sending data?
opts: A workspace key in config files
exp: The Azure Monitor Agent authenticates to Azure Monitor with a managed identity — system-assigned or user-assigned, or for Arc machines their Arc identity — so no workspace keys or secrets are stored. The legacy agent used a workspace ID and key.

q: What does enabling VM insights do?
opts: Installs AMA and creates a DCR that sends performance data
Enables disk encryption and sends its key logs to a workspace
exp: Enabling VM insights installs the Azure Monitor Agent (the older Dependency agent and Map feature are deprecated) and creates a data collection rule that sends performance data to a Log Analytics workspace. It doesn't turn on backup or encryption or add a public IP.

q: An existing deployment uses the deprecated Dependency agent. Which VM insights feature shows which servers a VM connects to and which processes listen on which ports?
exp: The Map feature of VM insights, which uses the Dependency agent, shows the processes running on each VM, the ports they listen on, and the inbound and outbound connections to other machines. Performance only shows charts, and workbooks are reports. Map and the Dependency agent retire on 30 June 2028, so don't enable them for new deployments.

q: Which experience shows network health, connectivity, traffic, and topology across subscriptions in one place?
exp: Network insights in Azure Monitor gives one view of network health, connectivity, traffic and topology for networking resources across subscriptions, with no setup. VM insights is for VMs, Storage insights is for storage, and Cost analysis is for spend.

q: Which service monitors live web application performance, failures, and dependencies through an SDK or auto-instrumentation?
exp: Application Insights is Azure Monitor's application performance monitoring (APM) feature. Through an SDK or auto-instrumentation it collects requests, response times, failures, exceptions and calls to dependencies from live web apps. VM insights monitors VMs, Network Watcher diagnoses networks, and Advisor gives recommendations.

q: You want an email when Azure has an outage or planned maintenance affecting your regions and services. Configure:
exp: A Service Health alert notifies you through an action group about Azure service issues, planned maintenance and health advisories that affect your subscriptions, regions and services. Metric alerts watch your own resources, budgets watch spend, and Resource Health covers individual resources.

q: What's the difference between Service Health and Resource Health?
opts: Service Health covers Azure service issues in regions; Resource Health shows the health of your individual resources
Resource Health covers Azure service issues in regions; Service Health shows the health of your individual VMs
Service Health is only for VMs
exp: Service Health tells you about problems with Azure services in the regions you use, such as outages and planned maintenance. Resource Health tells you whether your specific resource — for example VM1 — is available right now, and why not if it isn't. They're different views, and neither is about billing.

q: Which alert signal fires when a specific resource is deleted?
opts: Activity log alert on the delete operation
Log search alert on the Perf table
exp: An Activity log alert fires when a specific control-plane event happens, such as a delete operation on a resource or resource group. Metric alerts watch numeric values, log alerts on Perf watch performance data, and smart detection is an Application Insights feature.

q: A log search alert runs every 5 minutes over 5-minute windows but sometimes misses events. Why?
exp: Log data takes time to arrive in a workspace (ingestion latency, often a few minutes). If a rule checks the last 5 minutes every 5 minutes, late records can fall outside every window it evaluates and be missed. Use a longer window than the frequency, or allow for the delay.

q: Which alert severity is the most critical?
exp: Alert severities run from Sev 0 (Critical) through Sev 1 (Error), Sev 2 (Warning) and Sev 3 (Informational) to Sev 4 (Verbose). Sev 0 is the most critical — a lower number means a more serious alert.

q: Alerts should resolve automatically when CPU drops back below the threshold. Which option?
exp: With 'Automatically resolve alerts' enabled (stateful alerts), the alert's monitor condition changes to Resolved once the metric drops back below the threshold, and resolution notifications can be sent. Muting actions only silences notifications, processing rules change actions, and dynamic thresholds change how the threshold is calculated.

q: An alert must restart a VM automatically. Which action group action fits?
opts: An Automation runbook (or Logic App/Function) that restarts the VM
A voice call that asks the on-call engineer to restart the VM
exp: An action group can run an Azure Automation runbook (or a Logic App or Azure Function) that restarts the VM, so the alert fixes the problem automatically. Email and voice calls only notify people, and budgets track cost.

q: Which action group notification option emails users by RBAC role (for example, all subscription Owners)?
exp: The 'Email Azure Resource Manager role' notification sends email to everyone assigned a chosen role, such as Owner or Contributor, on the subscription. You don't have to maintain a list of addresses, because the recipients follow the role assignments. Plain email/SMS/push/voice needs fixed addresses, and webhooks and ITSM call systems, not people.

q: Order the steps to create a CPU alert that emails the ops team:
items: Create the alert rule: scope VM1, condition Percentage CPU > 85% for 5 min
Create an action group with the ops team email
Attach the action group to the alert rule and set severity
Test with a CPU spike or the Test action group feature
exp: First create the action group with the ops team's email, because an alert rule can only attach an action group that already exists. Then create the alert rule with its scope (VM1) and condition (CPU over 85% for 5 minutes), attach the action group and set the severity, and finally test it — for example with the 'Test action group' feature.

q: Which TWO can an alert processing rule do?
opts: Suppress action group notifications during a maintenance window
Add an action group to all alerts fired in a subscription
exp: Alert processing rules act on alerts after they fire: they can suppress action group notifications (for example during a maintenance window) or add action groups to every alert in a scope. They can't change an alert rule's condition or threshold, and they don't delete fired alerts.

ctx: VM1 has AMA with a DCR sending perf counters to LAW1. A metric alert (CPU > 90%) and a log search alert (free memory < 500 MB from Perf) both use action group AG-Ops.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: The CPU alert can fire within about a minute of the condition
The memory alert relies on data collected by AMA
Removing the DCR stops the memory alert from getting new data
AG-Ops can be shared by both alert rules
exp: Platform metrics such as CPU are near real-time, so the metric alert can fire within about a minute. Free memory is an in-guest counter collected by AMA through the DCR, so the log alert depends on it — remove the DCR and no new data arrives. One action group can be shared by many alert rules.
